title: Watts and Wesley
hookLine: two Englishmen wrote thousands of hymns still sung, like When I Survey and And Can It Be

cards: An English chapel, and a teenager named Isaac Watts sits in the pews, bored.
The churches he knew sang mainly the psalms, set into stiff rhymes, often lined out one line at a time by a leader and dragged back by the congregation.
The story goes that young Isaac complained, and his father said, more or less: then write something better. So he did. Hymn after hymn, some still sung at Christmas and on Good Friday.
A generation later, a restless Anglican priest named Charles Wesley would write thousands more. Between them, they gave English-speaking congregations a new kind of song.

teach.b: Hymn, from the Greek hymnos, a song of praise to a god or a hero. For Christians, it's a song of praise in verses, sung by the whole congregation.
Watts did something that sounds simple now and was daring then: new songs in plain English, in the voice of the people singing them, about the gospel. People call him the father of English hymnody.
He wrote Joy to the World and O God, Our Help in Ages Past.

And in 1707 he published When I Survey the Wondrous Cross. It walks slowly toward the cross, looks, and ends with the line that became today's carry: "Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all."
It doesn't argue. It just looks and answers. Then Charles Wesley.

He and his brother John started the movement that became the Methodists, and Charles wrote hymns by the thousand: Hark! the Herald Angels Sing, Love Divine, All Loves Excelling, and And Can It Be, written around his own conversion in 1738.
It's full of astonishment: "Amazing love! How can it be That Thou, my God, shouldst die for me?" One a careful poet, the other a fountain.
Watts was a Congregationalist, Wesley an Anglican, and their hymns now turn up in the hymnals of churches neither man belonged to.
Both keep landing on the same astonished word: amazing. A hymn is theology you can sing, in words plain enough that a tired congregation can carry it home.

how: Many churches sing hymns by Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley from printed hymnals or screens, especially at Christmas, Easter and funerals, and some Christians read hymns privately as poems or prayers.

games.q: who wrote what — tap the pairs.
p: When I Survey the Wondrous Cross

s: Watts and Wesley belonged to different churches
Watts was a Congregationalist; Charles Wesley was an Anglican priest. their hymns crossed church lines anyway.
Charles Wesley wrote only a handful of hymns
he wrote thousands, including Hark! the Herald Angels Sing and And Can It Be.
Watts and Wesley are only sung by Methodists
their hymns turn up in the hymnals of churches far beyond Methodism.

games.q: you're a teenager in church, bored by the singing, and you complain. your father says: then write something better. what do you do?
o: shrug it off and keep complaining.
write a new hymn for the next Sunday.
games.why: the story goes that young Isaac Watts did exactly that, and kept going, hymn after hymn. the story is told often; the details are hard to confirm.

practice: Say the last verse of When I Survey slowly, spoken, not sung, with a pause at every comma: "Were the whole realm of nature mine, That were a present far too small; Love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all."
Sit with it and let one word catch: realm, small, demands. If you pray, pray it back slowly; if you don't, read it as what it is, a man looking at something and finding his hands empty.

wordCard.voice: Hymn. From the Greek hymnos, a song of praise. A poem in verses, made for a whole congregation to sing.

orig.note: Greek: a song of praise, sung to a god or a hero. the English word hymn comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: love so amazing. Sung or simply spoken, it still lands just the same. Until tomorrow.
